newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Death and destruction on road to the Mai-Mai king.
newsitem.headline: Death and destruction on road to the Mai-Mai king.

text.p: On the road north from the town of Sake, toward the home of the mysterious Mai-Mai king, the signs of death and destruction are impossible to miss.

In the high green fields of the Masisi region, once a rich pasture for huge herds of cattle owned by Zairean Tutsis, Hutu militiamen left a trail of killing as they crossed the road westwards from the Rwandan border area in October.

Reporters penetrated the Masisi highlands on Friday for the first time since the conflict started, arguing their way through a checkpoint manned by the victorious rebels of the Rwandan-backed Alliance of Democratic Forces.
On the side of the road a family of seven lay dead in a bamboo grove, killed with machetes and bullets. The remains of a baby remained tied to its mother's back, its skull smashed by a machete.
Emmanuel Kambali, a resident of the Zairean border town of Goma on his way home after taking refuge in the Masisi, told the reporters of some of the bloody incidents in the highly complex conflict.

"On November 7 more than 500 Zaireans, trying to return to Sake, were massacred at Karamwetu by the Interahamwe," he said. Karamwetu is about 45 km (30 miles) north of Sake, and the Interahamwe are the Rwandan Hutu militia responsible for much of the genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994.

Other parties in the fighting have been the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces, the Zairean army, the present Rwandan army the RPF, the old Rwandan army, known as the FAR, and the Mai-Mai, a withcraft group traditionally hostile to all Rwandans but possibly now allied with the rebels.

"Near Karamwetu, at the village of Burunga, Tutsi forces from the RPF killed Rwandan Hutu refugees, but it was hard to tell who were civilians because the Interahamwe and the ex-FAR were all mixed up," said Kambali.
"At Karamwetu, there are bodies all over the tracks, in the mud and down the side of the hills," he added.

The Interahamwe are regrouping with elements of the Zairean army in Walikale, 110 km (65 miles) west of this area. That town and the strategic city of Kisangani further northwest are thought to be the next targets of the Alliance rebels.
The Mai-Mai has not gone public with its intentions but local residents say the Alliance rebels are recruiting them in large numbers to fight the ex-FAR and the Interahamwe.
"We call them the VABs," said one Zairean returning from the Masisi. "It means Vaccine Anti-Balles (anti-bullet vaccine) because they think their witchdoctor turns bullets into water."
"They like to wear strings of hands and feet around their necks," said one aid worker who worked in the region.
The Mai-Mai 'doctor' who provides the anti-bullet vaccine lives in Minova south of Sake and does not talk to the press.
